text:
Sampled HR@10 measures success against the pinned 99 negatives; it does not establish full-catalog ranking quality. Sampled metrics can even reverse model comparisons relative to full-catalog evaluation ([Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)). Keep users, candidates, splits and seeds unchanged. With 200 users/category, one additional hit changes category HR by 0.005 and the four-category macro-average by 0.00125.

Recommended adaptation of [paired bootstrap resampling](https://people.csail.mit.edu/koehn/publications/bootstrap2004.pdf): retain each model’s per-user binary hits, compute paired differences, resample 200 user pairs with replacement separately within each category, then average the four category differences equally. Report the observed macro difference, its bootstrap 95% interval and category differences. Resample stored outcomes only; no candidate regeneration or GPU training required. These intervals describe user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the fixed candidate assignments and trained checkpoints; they exclude training-seed variability, alternative negative samples and uncertainty across new datasets. If only aggregate HR is exposed, paired uncertainty cannot be recovered reliably.

Repeated checkpoint and hyperparameter selection can overfit finite validation data; ordinary intervals for the selected winner do not correct that selection bias ([Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)). Practical procedure: predeclare a bounded trial count, checkpoint evaluation schedule, stopping rule and deterministic tie-break within the GPU budget; log every evaluated checkpoint and select using the required macro HR@10. Use paired intervals as descriptive diagnostics, without claiming post-selection significance. Freeze the selected single checkpoint per category before the host’s final held-out evaluation; keep test outcomes unavailable throughout search.
